items.title: Why the Trump DOJ Is More of a Wreck Than Ever
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
A lot of things happened. Here are some of the things. This is TPM’s Morning Memo.

A Two-Tiered Justice Department

Before jumping into the news, I wanted to frame up quickly how to think about the current structure of the Justice Department as we head into the second half of Trump II.

The departures of some top political appointees from the Trump DOJ since the GOP was blown out in the midterms has gotten a lot of attention, but it’s been variously miscast, misunderstood, or mischaracterized.

The way the Justice Department historically worked was similar to every other department: A slate of political appointees was layered on top of the career employees to run the department and implement the president’s broad policy agenda. Those political appointees varied in terms of skill, professionalism, experience, and willingness to be independent versus do the White House’s bidding.

There were outliers — like Attorneys General John Mitchell and Bill Barr — but for the most part, the political appointees could be placed within a range that we might call “normal.” Then along came Trump II, and everything changed.

Attorneys General Pam Bondi and Todd Blanche exist far outside the normal range and have redefined what outliers are. They obliterated DOJ independence and participated in using the department as a sword against Trump’s foes and a shield for his friends.

They each surrounded themselves with a cadre of like-minded political appointees, but that circle is smaller than usual and has been getting steadily smaller. At this point, it’s down to Blanche, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, Associate Attorney General Stan Woodward, and Aakash Singh, the principal associate deputy attorney general. A former DOJer joked to the NYT that the Trump DOJ should be called “Four Guys” — a play on the burger chain’s name — to reflect its tiny leadership cadre.

Unlike past administration’s, the Trump II political appointees aren’t layered on top of the career employees in normal hierarchal fashion. They exist outside of that framework and in a posture not just adversarial to career employees but to some of the core functions of the department under the law, like public corruption and civil rights.

After the extensive Trump II purges of career employee, the political appointees now oversee a department Swiss-cheesed with a lack of capacity, abandoned units and sections, and absentee management. The only thing that keeps the department running in any recognizable form is that most of the day-to-day functioning of the DOJ happens in the 94 U.S attorney’s offices around the country. But they haven’t been spared either.

The rush for the exits among some political appointees post-election hasn’t really changed the core dynamic; it just more clearly reflects what was already going on. The department was already being run by the relative few remaining Trump true believers.

So small were there numbers and so preposterous their legal arguments that it’s been left to senior political appointees like Woodward to actually handle cases themselves, appearing in court, and earning the direct ire of federal judges. Woodward is defending inquiries in separate cases in D.C. and Chicago into whether the DOJ misled courts, and Woodward himself has come under withering criticism from judges.

The post-election departures have probably zapped some of the manpower that the political appointees have to handle cases directly themselves, although they’ve already shuffled in new attorneys to help. That’s a separate issue from the purges of career employees leaving DOJ beleaguered and under staffed, especially as it contends with a wave of immigrant habeas cases.

So when Singh — the conduit between Main Justice and the 94 U.S. attorneys — warned them after the election of firings to come and urged them to be on a “wartime footing,” it looked less like a powerful threat and more like flailing from a position of weakness.

While weakened, the Trump DOJ is no less dangerous after the election because it’s probably even more dysfunctional, unpredictable, and subordinate to the Trump White House.

Trump DOJ Sanctions Alert

A federal judge in the Eastern District of New York this week barred a Trump DOJ attorney from ever again appearing in a particular immigration case in front of him, Just Security reports. Two other DOJ attorneys in the case may suffer the same fate, the judge warned.

U.S. District Judge Sanket J. Bulsara said that a letter to the court from Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas Price was in “bad faith, a deliberate attempt to mislead the Court, perpetuate a fraud on the tribunal, and violate[s] obligations under Rule 11.”

The breach appears fatal to Price’s standing with the judge:

Judge Bulsara told Richard Hayes, head of the civil division at the U.S. Attorney’s office, that he should consider removing Price from other cases. “You should think about whether you want to swap him out and have some other lawyer from your office appear in any of his cases before me,” Judge Bulsara warned. “Your office is on notice.”

U.S. Attorneys Scheme: WDVA Edition

A criminal defendant is trying to disqualify Robert Tracci from acting as the top federal prosecutor in the Western District of Virginia, Bloomberg reports. Tracci’s appointment as first assistant U.S. Attorney came after the U.S. attorney position was already vacant, a circumstance which other courts have found insufficient to lawfully elevate the first assistant into the top post. It is one of the mechanisms that the Trump DOJ has used in its scheme to install loyalists as top federal prosecutors in blue states.

Stephen Miller Will Fail ‘Catastrophically’

Miles Taylor: “I spent the better part of two-and-a-half years dealing with Stephen Miller almost every day. And his selection [as White House chief of staff] is among the most dangerous, foolish, and self-defeating actions we’ve ever seen an American president take.”

Golf Course Case Heats Up

Ahead of a very contentious hearing this morning in the D.C. golf course case, the Trump DOJ told U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes that it objects to her plan to appoint a special master in the case. Reyes intends to have former D.C. U.S. Attorney Jessie Liu investigate whether the Trump DOJ or other government counsel misled the court in the case as a precursor to a potential contempt of court inquiry.

The hearing this morning started HOT — even though the hearing was ostensibly not about either the special master appointment or the DOJ’s alleged misconduct in the case. The immediate issue is that President Trump has ordered the closure of most of East Potomac Park, including the golf course, on Nov. 15, and the National Park Service plans to follow that direction. Plaintiffs are seeking a TRO to keep the park open.

Tying Up Some Loose Ends on the Election

: “In the run-up to the midterms, members of Georgia’s State Election Board and much of its professional staff were coordinating with an activist group led by Cleta Mitchell, the conservative attorney who worked with President Donald Trump to try to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election,” ProPublica reports.

The Big Lie of Noncitizen Voting: A federal magistrate judge in Wisconsin last week dismissed two voter fraud cases brought by the Trump DOJ. In each instance, the judge adopted a similar reasoning to a federal judge in Florida in a ruling last month. The gist is that the 40-year-old federal ban on noncitizen voting is unconstitutional because the states alone have the power to set voter qualifications in federal elections. The Florida case is on appeal, and there’s a lot more litigation coming over this. But it represents a big threat to Trump’s Big Lie of rampant noncitizen voting.

Politico: DHS messages back up allegations that Lewandowski operated as shadow secretary

NYT: “A Mexican former prosecutor facing arrest after allowing Central Intelligence Agency officers to operate in his state has fled to the United States and is now under the U.S. government’s protection, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.”

Next Week: Changes to Morning Memo

Tomorrow will mark four years since I took over writing Morning Memo. I assigned myself the task on what I thought would be a temporary basis until I found someone else to do it. It didn’t work out the way I expected.

That temporary fill-in ended up being the beginning of one of the most rewarding phases of my time here at TPM. At that point, I hadn’t written regularly in more than a decade, and I discovered how much I enjoyed the chance to do something directly myself rather than overseeing the doing of it by others.

Since then my role at TPM has evolved and so has the role of Morning Memo. Those changes accelerated in the first half of 2025 as we sailed into the teeth of the Trump II storm. Given the significance of the historical moment, Morning Memo gradually moved away from being a one-stop shop for all of the day’s essential political news and became instead a chronicle of the depredations of the Trump II presidency, with a special focus on the rule of law.

You may have also noticed the publishing time moved back closer to midday as the emphasis of Morning Memo changed from a rundown of the news to developing a taxonomy for and a shared narrative of the budding authoritarianism in America.

It became clear well before the election that it was time to repackage Morning Memo to better reflect what it has become. With the election past us, now’s the time to make the change. Beginning next week, “Morning Memo” will be renamed and its promise to you refined and updated.

Please welcome “Unsanctioned.”

I’ll be writing Unsanctioned every weekday. The substance of it will look very much like the Morning Memo of the past 22 months (which looked a bit different than the pre-Trump II version of Morning Memo that we started with). It will be repackaged and rebranded to reflect the new name and the new emphasis.

Among the changes, Unsanctioned will also offer extras exclusively to TPM members. It might be an extra edition on a busy news weekend or holiday. It might be a deeper dive on a topic or story than there’s room for in the standard version of Unsanctioned. It might be access to live interviews, additional news items, special news alerts, and other ways of serving you news and analysis.

If you were already receiving Morning Memo via email, you don’t need to do a thing to receive Unsanctioned. It will pop up in your inbox starting next week. If you have liked Morning Memo, you’ll feel right at home with Unsanctioned. And while I want to provide TPM members with additional ways to connect with Unsanctioned, non-members will still have access to what you’ve come to expect from me each weekday.

I’m looking forward to embarking together with you on this next phase for the country and for what I do here at TPM. I’m excited by the possibilities.

items.title: Donald Trump Will Do Anything to Get Ilhan Omar
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
A lot of things happened. Here are some of the things. This is TPM’s Morning Memo.

The Retribution: Somalia Edition

All of the discussion of the Trump White House’s resistance to oversight from the new Democratic Congress seems almost quaint in the context of the Trump DOJ raiding the home of a sitting Democratic member of Congress days before the election.

In a new development on that front, the NYT reports that the Trump administration took the unusual step of indicting one of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s former bodyguards in April for a felony related to his green card application in an attempt to flip him against her:

Mr. Mohamed’s lawyer, Bruce Rivers, said that prosecutors spent months trying to turn the bodyguard into an informant to bolster their case against Ms. Omar. In a move he described as shocking, Mr. Rivers said that prosecutors repeatedly told him and Mr. Mohamed that the investigation into Ms. Omar was “100 percent being run by 1600 Pennsylvania Ave.,” the address of the White House.

“I’ve never seen anything like this in my almost 28 years practicing law in federal court,” said Mr. Rivers, a veteran criminal defense lawyer in Minneapolis.

The case was by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Minnesota, but as the NYT notes: “The government lawyers assigned to the case were early-career federal prosecutors who were promoted to leadership roles in the U.S. attorney’s office in Minneapolis after several veteran attorneys left the office early this year in protest over its handling of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota.”

As the NYT puts it, the Trump DOJ “failed” to flip the bodyguard, but he was offered immunity and was brought before a D.C. grand jury investigating the Minnesota Democrat, where he reportedly testified to having no substantive knowledge of Omar’s immigration and marriage history.

The next day the Trump DOJ moved to dismiss the indictment, with the explanation from prosecutors that the bodyguard was in removal proceedings: “Accordingly, there is no longer a federal interest in continuing prosecution in light of his anticipated removal from the United States.” Take that as you will.

Before the election, Greg Sargent and Brian Beutler spoke to a number of House and Senate Democrats and senior aides about whether they were prepared for the extreme resistance to congressional oversight that the Trump White House was expected to demonstrate. Their conclusion:

Every Democrat we spoke with agreed that the Trump administration is world-historically corrupt, and most expected his lawbreaking to persist or even escalate. Some do seem willing to contemplate suspension of the regular order of things, if that’s what it takes to slow or stop the lawlessness. Others, though, seem more resigned to running a playbook for normal times, one that’s plainly unsuited to the coming moment.

The Trump White House resistance is already manifesting in absurd claims that congressional oversight is itself criminal.

Rep. Jared Huffman (D-CA), the ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, is demanding that the Interior Department preserve documents related to President Trump’s pet construction projects around D.C., CNN reports:

Multiple credible whistleblowers have approached Huffman’s committee in recent weeks to voice concern that the Interior Department is getting rid of records in anticipation of forthcoming scrutiny, the sources told CNN. The agency oversees much of the national parkland Trump wants to use for his projects.

The Interior Department called the whistleblower claims “100% false.”

Josh Marshall: Understanding the Scandal/Accountability Conveyor Belt

Still Basking in the Election Aftermath

A sampling of election news:

  • : Not a single Democratic incumbent in the House lost in the general election, the WaPo notes.

  • : Rep. Mike Turner (R-OH), who was swept out of office by the blue wave after nearly a quarter of a century in the House, blames his loss on that controversial ad by GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy: “That final ad from Vivek really was kind of a lightning strike at the end, and it had an impact up and down the ticket in all the races … Absolutely that was the margin at the end.”

  • : Democrats are one uncalled state Senate election away from having a trifecta in North Carolina. But in that very close race, state Sen. Danny Britt (R) still leads Catina Hamm (D) by 228 votes even though the race has tightened since election night. The race remains within the margin for a recount.

After all three levels of the federal courts blocked its lawsuit seeking to use the Big Lie of rampant noncitizen voting to interfere in the California election, the Trump DOJ moved to dismiss the case with a pissy filing complaining about all that losing.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter granted the dismissal, but not without taking a parting shot at the administration:

This lawsuit attempted to disrupt an ongoing election and create confusion and uncertainty for voters and election workers alike. The right to vote is sacred. So, too, is trust in our democracy. Upon recent receipt of the Department of Justice’s unilateral withdrawal of its Complaint in its entirety, and pursuant to the Department’s request, the expedited hearing this Court set regarding the validity of the government’s list for Friday, November 13, 2026 is now and hereby vacated. In light of the government’s withdrawal, this case is .

  • Fatal ICE Shooting in Maine: The ICE officer involved in a fatal shooting of a Colombia national in Maine over the summer previously expressed hatred of immigrants — especially Colombians — castigating his sister for her longtime relationship with a Colombian man, with whom she had two children, the NYT reports.

  • : Kim Wehle on how ICE is making immigrants vanish from its system.

  • : An ICE deportation carrying Iranian nationals to Pakistan, where they were to be handed over to Iran, turned around midair and landed back in Arizona after Pakistan refused to accept the detainees, sources tell the NYT.

What the Iran War Has Unleashed

  • In a new superseding indictment this week, federal prosecutors alleged that Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a leader of an Iranian-backed militia, passed along coded messages from jail in Brooklyn that were delivered to operatives working on behalf of Iran to target the Royal Air Force base at Fairford. In response to the alleged plot, the U.S. evacuated its military aircraft from the base last month.

  • In response to alleged Iranian threats against his life, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently moved out of his D.C. home and onto an unspecified nearby military base, the NYT reports.

One day after avoiding impeachment in the House, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth beclowned himself at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier:

Jensen Huang and Over-Concentration

Before Jensen Huang resigned this morning as the CEO of Nvidia, economist Justin Wolfers had used the scandal to show the dangerous concentration of power in one man at one company in one sector of the economy. It is parallel to (and overlapping with) the over-concentration of power in Donald Trump.

items.title: Why This Trump Lame-Duck Judicial Nomination Could be a Self-Own for the Ages
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
At Stake: Secret OLC Memos

The worst of the Trump II foreign misadventures were sanctioned by still-secret memoranda produced by the DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel — and now President Trump is poised to nominate the head of that office to fill a federal judgeship in Texas.

An Ohio native, Gaiser fits the mold for a Trump judge. He graduated from conservative Christian Hillsdale College and the University of Chicago School of Law. He clerked for diehard MAGA conservative judges Edith Jones on the 5th Circuit (his one notable connection to Texas), Neomi Rao on the D.C. Circuit, and Justice Samuel Alito. Gaiser was the solicitor general of Ohio before he joined the Justice Department last year.

Gaiser will now face a confirmation process in the Senate even as the House is moving toward a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — let this sink in — for overseeing military operations that the OLC under Gaiser blessed with some of its most controversial and still-secret memos.

    Against that backdrop, nominating Gaiser to the bench is an especially aggressive move. It gives senators newfound leverage to obtain the still-secret (or partially redacted) OLC memos which are suspected of having blessed (i) usurping Congress’ war powers; (ii) a boat-strike campaign that is viewed nearly universally by legal experts as a violation of international law and the rules of war; and (iii) the capture of Venezuela’s Maduro as a “law enforcement operation.”

    “The nomination of Gaiser for a judgeship is also likely to be, in significant part, a self-own,” NYU law professor Ryan Goodman noted yesterday. “It will very likely yield the public release of Gaiser/OLC opinions on (a) the boat strikes and (b) whatever convoluted magic the OLC concocted to say the Iran war was legal.”

    As Goodman pointed out, there is fairly recent precedent for senators using the leverage of a confirmation hearing to extract an OLC memo from an administration. Back in 2014, President Obama’s nomination of David J. Barron to the 1st Circuit gave a group of senators the chance to demand a secret OLC memo that justified drone strikes in Yemen that had killed four suspected terrorists who were U.S. citizens, including Anwar al-Awlaki. Barron had authored the memo while serving as the acting head of OLC. The Obama-era memo was turned over on the eve of Barron’s confirmation vote.

    Impeaching and even convicting Hegseth only gets you so much so long as Donald Trump remains president. Trump selects the next defense secretary, and the Pentagon — like the rest of the administration — is run out of the Trump White House.

    But a federal judgeship is different.

    Confirming Gaiser, just 37 years old, puts him on the federal bench for life. It potentially insulates him from further scrutiny for his conduct while at DOJ — in the same way that former acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove was safely ensconced on the Third Circuit Court of Appeals. Perhaps senators have learned a lesson since that fiasco. Perhaps not.

    : This item initially misidentified the circuit court on which Judge Barron sits.

    The Purges: Hegseth Google Edition

    Defense Secretary Hegseth’s office used Google searches for evidence of wokeness to weed out senior officers recommended for promotion as he purged the upper ranks of the military, MS Now reports:

    The senior official described to MS NOW how Hegseth’s executive office led a planned and deliberate process that involved creating paper-only files filled with printouts from internet searches that were inaccessible to the officers under consideration. Hegseth’s office gave instructions about the new criteria over the phone instead of in writing.

    The senior official described to MS NOW what was in the paper files for more than a dozen of the senior officers whose promotions were withheld. Some of the findings put into the paper-only files included officers who allowed a celebration that included rainbow flags, a Pride Month event and stood up a diversity committee and task force on the USS Kearsarge to combat discrimination.

    : On U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s watch, D.C. grand juries have refused to return indictments in three different cases in the past two weeks, the NYT reports. Two of the cases involved alleged voting fraud; one was the politicized prosecution of Trump I White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson.

    : The Trump DOJ is asserting various privileges rather than turn over some internal communications to U.S. District Judge April Perry in her inquiry into whether she was misled by DOJ attorneys in the since-abandoned prosecution of Operation Midway Blitz protesters. Or as Chicago Sun-Times reporter Jon Seidel wryly put it:

    Chicago U.S. Attorney’s office in March: “There are no communications … with anyone outside the [U.S. attorney’s office].”

    Main Justice today: “Please find a privilege log asserting privileges applicable to these communications.”

    : Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Floyd of Seattle, installed as part of President Trump’s U.S. attorney scheme, made a remarkable admission to the federal judges in the Western District of Washington. In a letter last week, Floyd said that his office is too overwhelmed to continue to contest each of the immigrant habeas cases filed in the flood of such cases unleashed by Trump’s mass deportation operation.

    US Aircraft Flee RAF Base Again

    For the second time in the last five weeks, the U.S. military has evacuated aircraft from a Royal Air Force base in the U.K. under potential threat from Iran.

    How the April car crash in Mexico that killed two CIA operatives blew the agency’s cover, triggered a national scandal south of the border, and sent the man who helped the CIA on the run.

    Lame-duck Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI) — a pariah in her own party after she endorsed (losing) GOP nominee Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race — was hard to find when Congress returned to Capitol yesterday. But she was eventually spotted hanging out in the Republican cloakroom.

items.title: Judge Plans To Appoint Special Master To Probe Trump DOJ Misconduct
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
The DOJ’s Absurd Caddyshack Moment

The D.C. golf course case continues to be a surprise contender for the long-awaited but elusive judicial branch showdown with the Trump administration over its chronic defiance of federal judges.

In an order over the weekend, U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes said she intends to appoint former D.C. U.S. Attorney Jessie K. Liu as a special master “to investigate whether Department of Justice or Department of the Interior counsel have committed ethical violations” in a lawsuit to block Trump’s renovation of the East Potomac Golf Course.

Reyes has been outraged at the Trump administration after deferring to it early in the case only to have it burn her later — a common pattern over the past 22 months of Trump II. An extensive tree-cutting operation on the golf course over the Columbus Day weekend was the proximate trigger for Reye’s ire, but a series of representations made to her in open court and in court filings have proven to be misleading at best and downright false at worst, she has found.

Liu’s investigation of Trump administration attorneys, including Stan Woodward, the No. 3 official at DOJ, will cover the period through Oct. 31, according to Reyes’ order, which offers this bio of Liu:

Ms. Liu served as the United States Attorney for the District of Columbia from 2017 to 2020, the same office in which she previously served as an assistant U.S. attorney. In addition, she has held senior positions at the Justice Department. These include deputy assistant attorney general in the Civil Rights Division; counsel to the deputy attorney general on national security issues; and deputy chief of staff for the National Security Division. Ms. Liu also served as deputy general counsel of the U.S. Department of the Treasury. In addition, Ms. Liu has been a partner at several international law firms. She is currently a partner at Liu Shur Kravis LLP.

Reyes gave the parties until Friday to raise any objections to Liu’s appointment (which will be at the government’s cost).

Trump DOJ Watch: Shitshow Edition

In addition to serving as a sword against Trump foes and a shield for his friends, the Trump DOJ under Attorney General Todd Blanche is an absolute zoo:

  • first told the White House in early October that she planned to resign as head of the Civil Rights Division after the election, but demanded that she be fired after he was displeased by her Oct. 18 appearance on “60 Minutes,” CBS News reports: “Justice Department officials were able to stall for time and allow her to proceed with her plans to resign after the election was over.”

  • , who was forced out as the assistant attorney general for the National Security Division, was called “Eisenblock” behind his back by then-Trump DOJ official , who now sits on the Third Circuit, Bloomberg reports: “Blanche briefly thought that was his actual surname before continuing using the moniker …”

  • The resignation of Miami U.S. Attorney may not have that dramatic of an immediate effect: “Many of the office’s most sensitive investigations were already being overseen by a top Blanche deputy, …” the NYT reports.

  • Associate Attorney General ’s “willingness to put his name behind controversial legal actions had led some officials to joke behind his back that his initials really stand for Sign Whatever,” the WSJ reports.

The Retribution: Post-Blowout Edition

Reeling from his midterm defeat, President Trump began threatening the new Democratic majority in Congress with imprisonment two months before it even takes office.

In two Truth Social posts over the weekend, Trump labelled as “extortion” Democratic threats of impeachment and promises of congressional oversight and demanded the Trump DOJ investigate: “By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately! President DONALD J. TRUMP”

The Retribution: NYT Edition

The Trump DOJ considered naming the NYT as an indicted co-conspirator in its third prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey.

In addition to all the grubby political retribution reasons for targeting the NYT, the Trump DOJ was desperately trying to get around a statute of limitations problem with charging Comey, the NYT reports: “The department’s consideration of treating The Times as a conspirator appeared to be an attempt to connect the Oct. 5, 2016, article with subsequent coverage by The Times involving Mr. Comey in a way that they contend could extend the statute of limitations.”

Late-stage radicalization and instability have characterized the actions and mood of autocrats in decline. We are seeing a version of it taking shape in the White House now. The Republican wipeout in the elections is prompting a dangerous reaction in a leader whose personality cult is shrinking and fading and whose foreign patrons are taking advantage of his weakness to make their influence over him more visible.

The Korematsu or Dred Scott of Our Time

“There are some opinions that I hope in my lifetime will get overturned. The immunity case is one of them.”—Trump v. U.S., which cloaked the president in a broad grant of immunity from criminal prosecution

Trump DOJ Dismisses CA Election Case

In a pissy filing, the Trump DOJ dismissed its lawsuit to force California election officials to segregate and not count the mail-in ballots of people who showed up on the department’s dubious list of 20,000 alleged noncitizens. The administration had suffered keys loses in the case at the district court, appeals court, and Supreme Court in the days before the election.

Kris Kobach Defeated In Kansas!

Longtime TPM fave Kris Kobach — an OG voter fraud bamboozler who later turned his attention to requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote — lost his re-election bid for Kansas attorney general.

More State Level Election Tidbits and Trivia

  • Not since Watergate … or Truman: “2026 will be the largest year for net gain in state legislative seats for Democrats since the 1974 Watergate Wave. As a percentage of seats, though, it’s looking like it’ll be the highest since Harry Truman’s election in 1948,” according to Chaz Nuttycombe, executive director of State Navigate.

  • : Democrats gained six new trifectas and broke five Republican ones. Heading into the election, Republicans held trifectas in 23 states, Democrats in 16. Coming out of the election, Democrats hold 22 trifectas and Republicans have 17, with Alaska still pending.

  • A rare cameo by the Whig Party: “In New York, Democrats are on track for their biggest state Senate majority since 1846, when they were running against the Whigs,” Politico reports.

The Trump administration is allegedly engaged in chain refoulement, the unlawful practice of using third countries to do the dirty work of returning immigrants to their country of origin when U.S. courts or immigration judges have barred their deportations, according to a NYT report:

But a New York Times investigation found that this program results in many of them being pushed back to the very countries where the Trump administration itself cannot legally send them. Some of the United States’ foreign partners have made clear that will happen. And when it does, the Trump administration continues sending planes full of deportees.

The Times identified more than 110 people who had court-ordered protections and were handed over to foreign governments, only to then be passed on to home countries where they risked torture, sexual abuse or persecution — risks that have been validated by American courts.

Rescued From the Memory Hole!

The new Democratic majority in the House will bring the Jan. 6 memorial plaque honoring defenders of the Capitol up from the basement to which House Republicans had relegated it.

items.title: The Tide Finally Turned Against the Depredations of the Trump II Presidency
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
We, the lucky ones, emerged this week from one of the darkest stretches in American history. The jubilation, the relief, the exhilaration are heartfelt and genuine and real and understandable. But not everyone who began this arduous journey with us was still around to celebrate its climactic conclusion.

Over the past 22 months, there have been innumerable tangible real world victims of the Trump II rampage: the millions of abandoned beneficiaries of USAID; the sick and dying betrayed by MAHA’s perverse notions of public health; the countless families ripped apart by indiscriminate mass deportation; the hundreds of immigrants dumped in countries with which they had no prior connection; the forgotten souls shipped off to foreign gulags; Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

There is no minimizing or excusing it. What they have lost is not recoverable. There is no making them whole again.

The COVID pandemic taught those of us who didn’t already know it the cruel lesson of how quickly humans forget and move on. Down deep, it may be a biological imperative, but we have refined it with a culture of short attention spans, a cultivated urgency to be always looking ahead, and an infinite ability to tell ourselves soothing and self-congratulatory stories about our own greatness.

Moments in history like these, when America redeems her lost promise, are uplifting and tantalizing with possibility — for those who survived what came before. The toils of slavery, the carnage of a civil war, the dehumanization of Jim Crow exacted extreme tolls in human misery and suffering, and the harrowing accounts of all but a very few individual victims are lost to history. There were in fact few happy endings.

In a culture that worships heroes, our stories are so full of them that I grew up internalizing that heroes were everywhere in every story and that all of us should be poised to be heroes in our own stories. It was only during COVID and the depredations of the Trump era that I finally came to see how rare heroes actually are and to understand that we are obsessed with heroes and with neat tidy Hollywood endings precisely because they are so rare in real life.

The heroes of the past nearly two years are not the people you’ve seen on TV or the pundits you’ve read or those who have delivered the loudest smackdowns of Trump. They weren’t posturing or preening. They were doing thankless tedious work that is neither glamorous nor lucrative. The work of democracy is boring, bureaucratic, and procedural — but essential all the same.

The heroes have been court staffs, paralegals, clerks, and junior associates working all night in emergency proceedings. They’ve been public interest lawyers, solo immigration attorneys, and immigrant advocates who were already familiar with the Kafkaesque immigration system even before Trump returned to office and made it infinitely worse.

Widening the circle, they’ve been health care providers, NGO workers, and arts administrators tirelessly endeavoring to preserve public services while fending off attacks. They’ve been parents struggling to provide normal childhoods to children who have been targeted because they’re brown or trans or disabled.

We, too, will move on in due course. But I didn’t want to do it yet without acknowledging who and what we’ve lost along the way.

I am deeply grateful that you have stuck with Morning Memo over the past two years. I did not make it easy on you.

I vowed not to sugarcoat the reality of Trump II but to chronicle it unstintingly. When things were at their most bewildering and hard to categorize in familiar ways, I threw enormous amounts of information at you. It was often raw and unsorted as I felt my way towards making sense of it all.

I refused, maybe stubbornly, to cast events in hopeful or optimistic terms unless they truly deserved it. I didn’t try to stuff events into artificial framings that fed the earnest desire for comeuppance, the hero’s revenge, or the villain’s fall.

It was a hard slog for readers. Many of you told me so. Morning Memo was difficult to read, hard to stomach, and relentless day after day for months on end.

Politics was grim. People wanted to avert their eyes. Many tuned politics outs or hit pause.

After a dramatic upswing in readership during the initial wave of Trump II atrocities in February and March 2025, it became hard to grow the audience for Morning Memo. The audience plateaued, but it didn’t shrink.

I feel a fierce pride in you for riding it out with me.

Trump II is not over yet. But we’ve clearly entered a new phase, with dramatically different power dynamics and a chance finally to move from a defensive crouch trying to protect what precious ground could be saved to taking the offensive and beginning to reclaim vast areas of American public life.

I look forward to navigating this next phase with you.

The Remaining Senate Races Edge Blue

: Scott Colom (D) has widened his lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R). The latest AP tally has him up by 1,936 votes, as the legal fight over the super-close election begins to take shape.

: The NYT projects that former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) is likely to sustain her narrow lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) even if she falls short of an outright majority and the election is decided on ranked choice. Meanwhile, President Trump wildly claimed that Sullivan should declare the winner.

Straight Into My Veins: Southern Gains

  • WSJ: The Red Wall Falls: Democrats Shatter Decades of GOP Dominance Across the South

Straight Into My Veins: Texas Sweep

  • Politico: Democratic Attorneys General Just Took Texas Off the Board: “We took the head of the snake.”

  • Texas Tribune: How schools could change for millions of students.

  • Politico: How Dems’ sweep in Texas blows up the 2028 map.

”I am not going to answer that question because that is a stupid question.”—longtime voter fraud bamboozler and election denier Cleta Mitchell, when asked by the NYT if she would join with President Trump in accepting the results of the 2026 election

Sher-ROD! I Will Never Unhear This ...

Trump DOJ Watch: Personnel Shuffle Edition

Some notable departures post-election from the Trump DOJ:

  • Miami U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones, who was overseeing the bogus investigation of the so-called “grand conspiracy” against Trump by the Deep State

  • Henry C. Whitaker, counselor to the attorney general, who among other things was handling the appeals in the James Comey and Letitia James prosecutions.

Be careful: No clear through line connects all of these departures, and there are often post-election personnel shuffles.

A Grim But Essential Read

Perhaps as a reminder that our struggles to preserve democracy have been more modest than we might like to admit: An incredible survival tale of one Ukrainian infantryman hunkered down alone on the front line against Russia as his body slowly disintegrated.

items.title: Has The Political Press Still Learned Nothing After a Decade of Trump?
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
It’s been a jangly 36 hours watching America rise up against a wannabe authoritarian while the political press resorts to the same old tired tropes as if it were hungry to go back to the pre-Trump days or pretend they never happened.

The U.S. press does a fine job covering democratic uprisings in foreign countries, but struggles mightily to cover them here at home.

While the midterm elections here fit neatly into a pattern of right-wing defeats in the past few weeks in Serbia and Brazil, the mainstream media here — even after a decade — is still grasping to employ suitable language for the current authoritarian moment in the United States.

The failures of the post-election news coverage mostly revolve around the embrace of worn-out horse-race campaign coverage and quickie post-election analysis in which losers lose because they’re idiots, and winners win because they’re geniuses.

The inability to grapple open and honestly with the Christian nationalist neo-fascism of the Trump II presidency continues to bedevil domestic political coverage. In one of its post-election analyses, the NYT allowed that it was “a decisive rebuke to President Trump and his aggressive, often chaotic second-term agenda.”

“Aggressive and often chaotic” are doing an awful lot of work there, as if the second term was an emotionally dis-regulated child with poorly medicated ADHD.

Contrast that with the NYT’s description of Viktor Orban’s election defeat in April, which it credited with “breaking the momentum of a global nationalist revival promoted by President Trump.” The Hungarian election, it reported, was a “showdown between friends and foes of liberal democracy.”

The coverage of an anodyne tweet by Vice President JD Vance yesterday captured the hunger of the political press to return to the coverage of old. Vance repeated what President Trump had already said — and what he would reaffirm after being asked about Vance’s tweet: that the Iran War cost them the election.

Yet that somehow that become evidence of a dramatic break between Vance and Trump — even though Vance conceded little, took blame for nothing, and whitewashed the entire rest of the “aggressive, often chaotic second-term agenda,” to borrow a phrase. Perhaps the Vance team self-servingly nudged reporters toward that interpretation, as the publication of a “tick-tock” of the tweet by Politico might suggest.

Blaming the Iran War is poised to become this cycle’s overly simplistic post-election narrative device. It offends almost no one, absolves the rest of the Trump II depredations, and misses its own anti-democratic origins.

We’re at risk of having the blue wave chalked up merely to the pocketbook impacts of the Iran War and the Trump tariffs without connecting either of them to the underlying authoritarianism involved.

The Iran War and the Trump tariffs, many of which (though not all) were struck down by the Supreme Court, were unilateral and illegal acts by the executive branch.

Trump sidelined Congress in violation of the constitutional order. These weren’t merely bad or poorly executed policies. The founders knew from experience that this is the folly you get from giving too much power to one man.

The notion that Republicans were victimized by Trump’s political “missteps” and “miscalculations” necessarily supposes that his rogue anti-democratic presidency is somehow disconnected from the horrible outcomes it produces. It also unwittingly implies that if the outcomes had been good, the means would have been fine.

It’s the Economy AND Corruption, Stupid

More Fun With Midterms Data

An assortment of interesting data points:

  • “Republicans have not won a House of Representatives ‌seat in ⁠a district that Trump carried by less than 11 percentage points two years ago. … Democrats have won four seats that Trump carried by more than 15 percentage points.”—

  • “Of about 3,000 counties where at least half the expected vote for the House has been tallied, all but about 170 saw Republican candidates run behind President Trump’s 2024 margin against Kamala Harris. The median county shifted about 11 percentage points toward the Democrats.”—

  • “Republicans are only on track to flip one House seat, in Maine, that they didn’t redraw last year.”—

Quote of the Day: Texas Edition

“Calling it a dummymander is generous. This was more like moron-mandering. We went for five seats, won none, killed an incumbent, and handed Democrats a reason to turn out. Was living with Henry Cuellar really that hard?”—an anonymous Texas GOP strategist whom Politico described as “frustrated”

Chart of the Day: Texas Edition

Democrats swept every demographic and geographic subgroup, according to the Times Voter Trends, except these (with the margin for Republicans):

    Impact on the New Congress

    Despite the Supreme Court’s decision in and subsequent aggressive Republican mid-decade redistricting to eliminate Black majority-minority districts, the impact on the new Congress is more nuanced than I might have expected.

    • A total of 8 seats are going from Black to non-Black members, but four of those were held by Black Republicans, three of whom ran for higher office.

    • A total of 6 seats are going from non-Black to Black members.

    • Two Black members targeted by the GOP mid-decade redistricting scheme appear likely to survive: Shomari Figures (D-AL) and Don Davis (D-NC).

    The blue wave unquestionably muted the effects of … and I can’t emphasize this enough … .

    Before anyone interprets these numbers as minimizing what’s happened to Black voter representation in the South, was always understood to have more dramatic effects on state and local representation than on Congress. One of its biggest knock-on effects is to deprive Black candidates of access to the lower rungs of the political ladder that they can use to reach Congress.

    It’s also important to remember that the Voting Rights Act was about empowering Black , not Black candidates — so diversity among electeds is only a rough proxy for Black political power.

    This all comes against the backdrop of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) being poised to become the first Black speaker of the House and the addition of Juliana Stratton (D-IL) giving the Senate a record number of six Black senators, with a seventh if Scott Colom (D) wins in Mississippi.

    Mike Johnson Won’t Return as GOP Leader

    Outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) won’t seek to return as the House GOP leader in the next Congress, leaving Majority Leader Steve Scalise (LA) and Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (OH) to duke it out.

    This WaPo headline is a false dichotomy often used to manufacture storylines in political coverage: “Democrats face a choice on Trump come January: Confrontation or compromise.”

    Confrontation v. compromise is as flat, reductive, and imprecise as most of the dreary analysis of the moderate v. progressive fault line within the Democratic Party. There is understandable hunger for the prototypical Democratic officeholder to be more robust, combative, and decisive; but this kind of thin analysis sets up an easy gotcha for subsequent coverage that doesn’t reflect the strength of Democrats’ new majorities on the Hill.

    The reality is Democrats do not face a stark choice between confrontation and compromise. The can do both or either or neither. They get to pick when and where to fight their battles. They get to decide which hills to die on. They are in the driver’s seat.

    Besieged District Courts Get Relief

    Georgetown law professor Steve Vladeck, on the critical relief that a Democratic Congress can provide federal district courts:

    [T]he district courts have been under siege—even as they have been instrumental in standing up for the rule of law by fighting a classic rear-guard action. Unlike Blanche, they haven’t been trying to win a “war,” but rather just trying to hold the line in the hope that reinforcements would eventually be on their way.

    Thanks to Tuesday’s election results, those reinforcements are coming—in the form of a House of Representatives and Senate that will be just as interested in checking the executive branch …

    Races to Watch: Schadenfreude Edition

    Obviously all eyes remain on the Mississippi and Alaska Senate races, which still hang in the balance, but longtime TPM readers will want to keep an eye on two House races that remain too close to call:

    : Republican Rep. , 48%, is trailing Democrat Eileen Laubacher, 48.7%, with 93% of the votes counted. Boebert, first elected to Congress in 2020, has been the archetypical MAGA-era GOP House member: a transgressive, attention-seeking wild child with a messy personal life.

    : Rep. (R) is trailing by 280 votes against Democrat Victoria Broderick, with 99% of the votes counted. DesJarlais predates the Trump era, having arrived in the Tea Party wave of 2010. He has persisted, shall we say, despite his own personal messiness being exposed earlier in his congressional career.
